source_text: Quoquo tamen, inquis, modo substantia creatoris delicti capax inuenitur, cum adflatus dei, id est anima, in homine deliquit nec potest non ad originalem summam referri corruptio portionis. ad hoc interpretanda erit qualitas animae. inprimis tenendum quod Graeca scriptura signauit, adflatum nominans, non spiritum. quidam enim de Graeco interpretantes non recogitata differentia nec curata proprietate uerborum pro adflatu spiritum ponunt et dant haereticis occasionem spiritum dei delicto infuscandi, id est ipsum deum. et usurpata iam quaestio est. intellege itaque adflatum minorem spiritu esse. ut aurulam eius, et si de spiritu accidit, non tamen spiritum. nam et aura uento rarior, et si de uento aura, non tamen uentus. [aura] capit etiam imaginem spiritus dicere flatum. nam et ideo homo imago dei, id est spiritus; deus enim spiritus. imago ergo spiritus flatus. porro imago ueritati non usquequaque adaequabitur. aliud est enim secundum ueritatem esse, aliud ipsam ueritatem esse. sic et adflatus, cum imago sit spiritus, non potest ita imaginem dei comparare, ut, quia ueritas, id est spiritus, id est deus, sine delicto est, ideo et imago, id est adflatus, (id est homo,) non debuerit admisisse delictum. in hoc erit imago minor ueritate et adflatus spiritu inferior, habens illas utique lineas dei, qua inmortalis, [anima] qua libera et sui arbitrii, qua praescia plerumque, qua rationalis, capax intellectus et scientiae, tamen et in his imago et non usque ad ipsam uim diuinitatis; sic nec usque ad integritatem a delicto, quia hoc soli deo cedit, id est ueritati. et hoc solum imagini non licet. sicut enim imago, cum omnes lineas exprimat ueritatis, ui tamen ipsa caret, non habens motum, ita et anima, imago spiritus, solam uim eius exprimere non ualuit, id est non delinquendi felicitatem. ceterum non esset anima, sed spiritus, nec homo qui animam sortitus est, sed deus. et alias autem non omne, quod dei erit, deus habebitur, ut expostules deum et adflatum, id est uacuum a delicto, quia dei sit adflatus. nec tu enim, si in tibiam flaueris. hominem tibiam feceris, quamquam de anima tua flaueris. sicut et deus de spiritu suo. denique cum manifeste scriptura dicat flasse deum in faciem hominis et factum hominem in animam uiuam, non in spiritum uiuificatorem, separauit eam a condicione factoris. opus enim aliud sit necesse est ab artifice, id est inferius artifice. nec urceus enim factus a figulo ipse erit figulus; ita nec adflatus factus a spiritu ideo erit spiritus. ipsum quod anima uocitatus est flatus, uide, ne etiam de adflatus condicione transierit in aliquam diminutiorem qualitatem. ergo, inquis, dedisti animae infirmitatem supra negatam. plane, cum illam exigis deo parem, id est delicti inmunem, dico infirmam; cum uero ad angelum prouocatur, fortiorem defendam necesse est dominum uniuersitatis, cui iam angeli administrant, qui etiam angelos iudicaturus est, si in dei lege constiterit, quod in primordio noluit. hoc ipsum ergo potuit adflatus dei admittere; potuit, sed non debuit. potuisse enim habuit per substantiae exilitatem, qua adflatus, non spiritus, non debuisse autem per arbitrii potestatem, qua liber, non seruus, adsistente amplius demonstratione non delinquendi sub comminatione moriendi, qua substrueretur substantiae exilitas et regeretur sententiae libertas. itaque non per illud iam uideri potest anima deliquisse, quod illi cum deo adfine est. id est per adflatum, sed per illud, quod substantiae accessit. id est per liberum arbitrium, a deo quidem rationaliter adtributum, ab homine uero qua uoluit agitatum. quod si ita se habet, omnis iam dei dispositio de mali exprobratione purgatur. libertas enim arbitrii non ei culpam suam respuet, a quo data est, sed a quo non ut debuit administrata est. quod denique malum describes creatori?si delictum hominis, non erit dei quod est hominis, nec idem habendus est delicti auctor qui inuenitur interdictor, immo et condemnator. si mors malum, nec mors comminatori suo, sed contemptori faciet inuidiam. ut auctori. contemnendo enim eam fecit, non utique futuram, si non contempsisset.
pass_a_gloss: In whatever way, you ask, the substance of the Creator is found capable of sin, since the breath of God, that is the soul, sins in man and cannot but be referred back to the original sum of corruption of a part. For this reason, the quality of the soul will have to be interpreted. First, it must be held that the Greek Scripture has signified, naming the breath, not the spirit. For some, interpreting from Greek, not having considered the difference nor taken care of the property of words, put spirit in place of breath and give heretics the opportunity to obscure the spirit of God with sin, that is, God Himself. And the question has already been usurped. Understand, therefore, that the breath is less than the spirit. Just as a small part of gold is not the whole, and if it happens to be from the spirit, it is not nevertheless the spirit. For even the breeze is rarer than the wind, and if the breeze is from the wind, it is not nevertheless the wind. The breeze can also be said to be an image of the spirit, that is, breath. For man is the image of God, that is, the spirit; for God is spirit. Therefore, the image of the spirit is breath. Furthermore, the image will not be entirely adequate to the truth. For it is one thing to be according to the truth, another to be the truth itself. So also the breath, since it is the image of the spirit, cannot compare to the image of God in such a way that, because the truth, that is, the spirit, that is, God, is without sin, therefore the image, that is, the breath, (that is, man,) ought not to have admitted sin. In this, the image will be less than the truth, and the breath inferior to the spirit, having, to be sure, those lines of God, in that it is immortal, in that it is free and of its own will, in that it is often prescient, in that it is rational, capable of intellect and knowledge, yet even in these things, the image and not up to the very power of divinity; so also not up to the integrity of being without sin, because this belongs to God alone, that is, to the truth. And this alone is not permitted to the image. For just as the image, when it expresses all the lines of truth, nevertheless lacks the power itself, not having motion, so also the soul, the image of the spirit, was not able to express its power alone, that is, the happiness of not sinning. Otherwise, it would not be the soul, but the spirit, and not man, who has been allotted the soul, but God. And besides, not everything that is God's will be considered God, so that you might expostulate that God and the breath, that is, the one free from sin, are the same, because the breath is God's. Nor, if you blow into a flute, do you make the flute a man, although you blow with your soul. Just as God also blows with His spirit. Finally, since Scripture clearly says that God blew into the face of man and man was made into a living soul, not into a life-giving spirit, it separated the soul from the condition of the Creator. For the work must necessarily be different from the artisan, that is, inferior to the artisan. Nor is the jar made by the potter the potter itself; so also the breath made by the spirit is not the spirit. The fact that the soul is called breath, see that it does not also pass into a lesser quality from the condition of the breath. Therefore, you ask, have I given the soul infirmity, which was denied above? Certainly, when you demand that it be equal to God, that is, immune from sin, I say it is infirm; but when it is compared to an angel, I must defend it as stronger, the Lord of the universe, to whom the angels already minister, who will also judge the angels, if they stand in God's law, which they did not want in the beginning. This, therefore, the breath of God was able to admit; it was able, but it ought not to have. For it had the ability through the thinness of its substance, in that it is breath, not spirit, but it ought not to have through the power of its will, in that it is free, not a servant, with the additional demonstration of not sinning under the threat of death, by which the thinness of the substance would be supported and the freedom of the sentence would be ruled. Therefore, it cannot be seen that the soul sinned because of that which is akin to God, that is, through the breath, but through that which was added to the substance, that is, through free will, which was rationally given by God, but was acted upon by man as he willed. But if this is the case, God's entire disposition is already purged of the reproach of evil. For the freedom of the will does not reject its own guilt from the one who gave it, but from the one who did not administer it as he ought. What evil, finally, do you describe to the Creator? If it is the sin of man, it will not be God's, which is man's, nor will the same one be considered the author of sin who is found to be the prohibitor, indeed even the condemner. If death is evil, death will not bring shame to its comminator, but to its contemner. Just as to the author, for by contempt, he made it, not, to be sure, as something that would be, if it had not been contemned.

choices.why: to refer to the human soul

bible_refs.note: God blew into the face of man and man was made into a living soul

pass_b_english: However you put it, you ask, the Creator's substance is found capable of sin, since God's breath—that is, the soul—sinned in man, and the corruption of a part cannot help but be traced back to the original total. That is why the soul's quality must be explained. First, we must hold that Greek Scripture uses 'breath,' not 'spirit.' Some translators from Greek, ignoring the distinction and careless with word choice, substitute 'spirit' for 'breath' and hand heretics the chance to smear God's Spirit with sin—that is, to smear God Himself. The question has already been hijacked. So understand: breath is less than spirit. A scrap of gold is not the whole, even if it comes from the spirit, it is still not the spirit. A breeze is rarer than wind; even if the breeze comes from the wind, it is not the wind. 'Breath' can also be called an image of the spirit. For man is the image of God—that is, the Spirit; God is Spirit (John 4:24). Therefore the image of the Spirit is breath. Moreover, an image never fully matches the truth. Being 'according to the truth' is one thing; being the truth itself is another. So the breath, as the Spirit's image, cannot claim the image of God in such a way that, because the truth—that is, the Spirit, that is, God—is sinless, the image—that is, the breath, that is, man—should not have admitted sin. Here the image falls short of the truth, and the breath is inferior to the Spirit, even though it bears God's lines: immortality, freedom and self-determination, frequent prescience, rationality, capacity for intellect and knowledge. Yet even in these it remains an image, not the very power of divinity; so also it does not reach the integrity of sinlessness, because that belongs to God alone, that is, to the truth. And that integrity is the one thing denied to an image. Just as an image reproduces every line of the truth yet lacks the power itself—it has no motion—so the soul, the Spirit's image, could not express the Spirit's power alone, namely the happiness of not sinning. Otherwise it would not be a soul but the Spirit, and the being who received a soul would not be man but God. Besides, not everything that belongs to God is God, so you cannot demand that God and the breath—that is, the one free from sin—are identical just because the breath is God's. If you blow into a flute, you do not make the flute a man, even though you blow with your soul. God likewise blows with His Spirit. Finally, since Scripture plainly says God breathed into man's face and man became a living soul, not a life-giving spirit (Genesis 2:7), it separated the soul from the Creator's condition. The work must necessarily differ from the artisan—be inferior to the artisan. The jar the potter makes is not the potter; so the breath made by the Spirit is not the Spirit. The very fact that the soul is called 'breath' warns that it may have slipped into an even lesser quality than the condition of breath implies. So you ask: have I granted the soul a weakness I denied above? Absolutely. When you demand it be God's equal—that is, immune from sin—I call it weak; but when it is matched against an angel, I must defend it as stronger, the Lord of the universe, to whom angels already minister, who will also judge angels if they stand in God's law, which they refused at the start. Therefore God's breath was able to admit sin; it was able, but it ought not to have. It had the ability through the thinness of its substance—being breath, not Spirit—but it ought not to have through the power of its will—being free, not a slave—with the added demonstration of not sinning under the threat of death, by which the substance's thinness would be reinforced and the freedom of the decree governed. Consequently, it cannot be seen that the soul sinned because of what is akin to God—that is, through the breath—but through what was added to the substance: free will, rationally given by God, but exercised by man as he chose. If this stands, God's entire ordering is cleared of the reproach of evil. The freedom of the will does not shift its guilt onto the one who gave it, but onto the one who did not administer it as he should. What evil, finally, do you pin on the Creator? If it is man's sin, it is not God's, which is man's; nor is the same one the author of sin who is found to be its prohibitor, indeed its condemner. If death is evil, death brings shame not on its threatener but on its contemptor—just as on the author; for by contempt he made it happen, not as something inevitable if it had not been despised.
